48: 2 REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC KDV EQUATION
49: tools that were developed over the past decade and half for invest igating dispersive partial
50: diﬀerential equations (see the discussion and references mention ed below). Moreover, we
51: also remark that the tools and ideas that are developed in this contr ibution can be easily
52: applied to multi-dimensional equations and multi-component systems , a subject of future
53: investigation.
54: It is worth mentioning that similar approach, taking advantage of tim e averaging, has
55: also been applied to the two-dimensional rotating inviscid Burgers eq uations in [1] and
56: [16] to show that fast rotation prevents the formation of a ﬁnite t ime singularity in the
57: two-dimensional Burgers system. We will use this warmup toy model, and in particular
58: the approach in [1], to ﬁx ideas and to illustrate in section 2 the averag ing mechanism,
59: which is instrumental in regularizing the solutions and in preventing th e formation of a
60: ﬁnite time singularity for the two-dimensional inviscid Burgers syste m.
61: Our approach consists of three steps. First, we rewrite the prob lem as a system of
62: ODE for time-dependent Fourier coeﬃcients. This is a standard app roach to the periodic
63: problem which is commonly used. Second, to make the eﬀects of time a veraging explicit
64: we single out oscillating factors and do several integration by parts , with respect to time,
65: to obtain several generations of equations for slowly varying coeﬃ cients. Resonances
66: reveal themselves as obstacles to the integrations by parts and p roduce resonant terms
67: in the equations, integrated terms become more and more regular. Higher generations of
68: equations allow solutions with less regularity. This algorithm is simple and straightforward,
69: it does not use ﬁne methods such as analytic reduction to linear form s and analysis of self
70: similar solutions or the construction of conserved or almost conser ved quantities. The third
71: step is analysis of the obtained equations. To show their regularity w e use straightforward
72: estimates of multilinear operators, energy estimates and the Cont raction principle. To use
73: the contraction principle in negative Sobolev spaces we use splitting t o high and low Fourier
74: modes and exploit averaging-induced squeezing of higher modes. In order to justify our
75: estimates we use a Galerkin approximations procedure. We try to us e methods which can
76: be easily adjusted to general multidimensional problems such as tho se mentioned above
77: in hydrodynamic problems. We do not use in our analysis the speciﬁc pr operties of the
78: KdV equation such as complete integrability or special conserved qu antities. Moreover,
79: one can expect that in order to obtain more delicate information one has to resort to the
80: use of higher generations of equations, i.e. more integrations by pa rt.
81: The paper is organized as follows. In section 3 we reformulate the Kd V equation in
82: terms of its Fourier components and introduce the notion of weak s olution; we also make
83: two types of formal transformations of the equation which will be u sed for proving the
84: relevant well-posedness results. In section 4 we use the Galerkin pr ocedure for proving the
85: global existence in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s >0. In section 5 we use the Contraction
86: Principle to show that the solutions established in section 4 are unique and Lipschitz
87: continuous, with respect to the initial data, in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s ≥ 1/2. A
88: more technical section 6 is devoted to proving similar results for s ∈ [0, 1/2], where the
89: case s = 0 is dealt with separately. Finally, for solutions with initial data in L2 we show
90: the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these solutions, with resp ect to the initial data,
91: as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s for all s ∈ (−1, 0].
92: There is a long history of the KdV equations in the periodical setting. We do not attempt
93: to give here a complete survey of this long history, but we are satisﬁ ed by mentioning,
94: below, some of the key landmark results. First Bourgain [6] proved local well-posedness in
95: L2. We observe that the result of Bourgain also implies global existence for the real valued
96: KdV in L2. Later the local well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s > −1/2, was
97: 
98: REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC KDV EQUATION 3
99: established for the real and complex valued KdV by Kenig, Ponce, an d Vega [14]. Later
100: global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1/2, was established for the real
101: valued KdV by Colliander, Keel, Staﬃlani, Takaoka and Tao [7]. Using th e fact that the
102: KdV equation is an integrable system, and by implementing the inverse method, Kappeler
103: and Topalov [15] proved global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1.
104: Even though the results presented in this contribution are weaker than the state-of-the-
105: art results mentioned above, our approach is substantially diﬀeren t and easy to master.
106: Speciﬁcally, and as we have stressed above, our approach is based on systematic applica-
107: tion of time averaging. It is worth mentioning that since we rewrite th e KdV equation
108: in diﬀerent forms, based on the diﬀerentiation by parts with respec t to the time variable,
109: there is superﬁcial similarity with the reduction to normal forms (cf . [19]). The diﬀerence
110: is that the consecutive forms of the KdV, which we derive, are base d not on the geometric
111: properties such as a reduction to a linear form or a reduction to inva riant tori, but ex-
112: clusively on time averaging properties. In order to stress the eﬀec ts, which are due solely
113: to the time averaging, we do not use energy conservation or modiﬁe d energy functionals
114: as in the I-method. We use only the L2 norm conservation to mimic the situation which
115: occurs in the three-dimensional Euler equations and other hydrod ynamical systems.
116: Moreover, we believe that the averaging approach presented her e can be pushed further
117: to achieve the best known results concerning the KdV equation. Fu rthermore, diﬀerent
118: nonlinear dispersive and wave equations, such as the m-KdV, the Kle in-Gordon equation
119: and water wave equations (see for example, [13], [19], [23]-[25], and re ferences therein),
120: can possibly be studied quite similarly, a subject of future research .

2: ON THE REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC
3: KORTEWEG–DE VRIES EQUATION
4: Anatoli V. Babin 1, Alexei A. Ilyin 2 and Edriss S. Titi 3
5: This paper is dedicated to the memory of Professor Basil Nicolaenko
6: Abstract. In this paper we develop and use successive averaging method s for explaining the regular-
7: ization mechanism in the the periodic Korteweg–de Vries (Kd V) equation in the homogeneous Sobolev
8: spaces ˙H s, for s ≥ 0. Speciﬁcally, we prove the global existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz continuous
9: dependence on the initial data of the solutions of the period ic KdV. For the case where the initial data
10: is in L2 we also show the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these so lutions with respect to the initial
11: data as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s, for s ∈ (−1, 0].
12: Keywords: Korteweg–de Vries equation, dispersive equations, averaging met hod, non-
13: linear resonance.
14: MSC: 35B34,35Q53.
15: 1. Introduction
16: This paper is motivated by works on global regularity of solutions of 3 D problems in
17: hydrodynamics (Navier-Stokes or Boussinesq system with periodic boundary conditions)
18: in the presence of fast rotation or strong stratiﬁcation, see, e.g ., [1], [2], [3], [4], [11],
19: [12], [18], [16], [20], [26], and references therein. The results are base d on the presence of
20: high-frequency waves that lead to destructive interference and eﬀectively weaken the non-
21: linearity through time averaging allowing to prove global regularity of solutions for these
22: problems, at the limit of inﬁnite rotation. The above mentioned hydro dynamical problems
23: are rather complicated (Boussinesq system, for example, involves ﬁve unknown functions of
24: three spatial variables and time, the equations are coupled throug h a quadratic nonlinear-
25: ity). Therefore, the purpose of this paper is to apply this averagin g approach to a slightly
26: simpler problem to make these ideas more transparent. Here we con sider the Korteweg–de
27: Vries equation with one spatial variable subjected to periodic bound ary condition. The
28: averaging eﬀects are strong because on high Fourier modes the line ar term generates high-
29: frequency oscillations which weakens the nonlinearity and makes it mild er. In this paper
30: we show connections between the smoothness properties of solut ions of the Korteweg–de
31: Vries (KdV) equation and the algebraic structure of the nonlinear r esonances between the
32: high-frequency oscillations. Our main goal is to make the relations be tween time-averaging
33: eﬀects and smoothness issues more explicit, rather than to obtain global regularity results
34: under minimal restrictions (see, e.g., [5], [7], [14] and the references therein). In particular,
35: our approach and aim are completely diﬀerent than the machinery an d harmonic analysis
36: Date: Submitted: November 3, 2009. Revised: October 22, 2010. T o appear in: Communications in
37: Pure and Applied Mathematics.

48: 2 REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC KDV EQUATION
49: tools that were developed over the past decade and half for invest igating dispersive partial
50: diﬀerential equations (see the discussion and references mention ed below). Moreover, we
51: also remark that the tools and ideas that are developed in this contr ibution can be easily
52: applied to multi-dimensional equations and multi-component systems , a subject of future
53: investigation.
54: It is worth mentioning that similar approach, taking advantage of tim e averaging, has
55: also been applied to the two-dimensional rotating inviscid Burgers eq uations in [1] and
56: [16] to show that fast rotation prevents the formation of a ﬁnite t ime singularity in the
57: two-dimensional Burgers system. We will use this warmup toy model, and in particular
58: the approach in [1], to ﬁx ideas and to illustrate in section 2 the averag ing mechanism,
59: which is instrumental in regularizing the solutions and in preventing th e formation of a
60: ﬁnite time singularity for the two-dimensional inviscid Burgers syste m.
61: Our approach consists of three steps. First, we rewrite the prob lem as a system of
62: ODE for time-dependent Fourier coeﬃcients. This is a standard app roach to the periodic
63: problem which is commonly used. Second, to make the eﬀects of time a veraging explicit
64: we single out oscillating factors and do several integration by parts , with respect to time,
65: to obtain several generations of equations for slowly varying coeﬃ cients. Resonances
66: reveal themselves as obstacles to the integrations by parts and p roduce resonant terms
67: in the equations, integrated terms become more and more regular. Higher generations of
68: equations allow solutions with less regularity. This algorithm is simple and straightforward,
69: it does not use ﬁne methods such as analytic reduction to linear form s and analysis of self
70: similar solutions or the construction of conserved or almost conser ved quantities. The third
71: step is analysis of the obtained equations. To show their regularity w e use straightforward
72: estimates of multilinear operators, energy estimates and the Cont raction principle. To use
73: the contraction principle in negative Sobolev spaces we use splitting t o high and low Fourier
74: modes and exploit averaging-induced squeezing of higher modes. In order to justify our
75: estimates we use a Galerkin approximations procedure. We try to us e methods which can
76: be easily adjusted to general multidimensional problems such as tho se mentioned above
77: in hydrodynamic problems. We do not use in our analysis the speciﬁc pr operties of the
78: KdV equation such as complete integrability or special conserved qu antities. Moreover,
79: one can expect that in order to obtain more delicate information one has to resort to the
80: use of higher generations of equations, i.e. more integrations by pa rt.
81: The paper is organized as follows. In section 3 we reformulate the Kd V equation in
82: terms of its Fourier components and introduce the notion of weak s olution; we also make
83: two types of formal transformations of the equation which will be u sed for proving the
84: relevant well-posedness results. In section 4 we use the Galerkin pr ocedure for proving the
85: global existence in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s >0. In section 5 we use the Contraction
86: Principle to show that the solutions established in section 4 are unique and Lipschitz
87: continuous, with respect to the initial data, in the Sobolev spaces ˙H s for s ≥ 1/2. A
88: more technical section 6 is devoted to proving similar results for s ∈ [0, 1/2], where the
89: case s = 0 is dealt with separately. Finally, for solutions with initial data in L2 we show
90: the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these solutions, with resp ect to the initial data,
91: as maps from ˙H s to ˙H s for all s ∈ (−1, 0].
92: There is a long history of the KdV equations in the periodical setting. We do not attempt
93: to give here a complete survey of this long history, but we are satisﬁ ed by mentioning,
94: below, some of the key landmark results. First Bourgain [6] proved local well-posedness in
95: L2. We observe that the result of Bourgain also implies global existence for the real valued
96: KdV in L2. Later the local well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s > −1/2, was
97: 
98: REGULARIZATION MECHANISM FOR THE PERIODIC KDV EQUATION 3
99: established for the real and complex valued KdV by Kenig, Ponce, an d Vega [14]. Later
100: global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1/2, was established for the real
101: valued KdV by Colliander, Keel, Staﬃlani, Takaoka and Tao [7]. Using th e fact that the
102: KdV equation is an integrable system, and by implementing the inverse method, Kappeler
103: and Topalov [15] proved global well-posedness in the Sobolev space H s, for s> −1.
104: Even though the results presented in this contribution are weaker than the state-of-the-
105: art results mentioned above, our approach is substantially diﬀeren t and easy to master.
106: Speciﬁcally, and as we have stressed above, our approach is based on systematic applica-
107: tion of time averaging. It is worth mentioning that since we rewrite th e KdV equation
108: in diﬀerent forms, based on the diﬀerentiation by parts with respec t to the time variable,
109: there is superﬁcial similarity with the reduction to normal forms (cf . [19]). The diﬀerence
110: is that the consecutive forms of the KdV, which we derive, are base d not on the geometric
111: properties such as a reduction to a linear form or a reduction to inva riant tori, but ex-
112: clusively on time averaging properties. In order to stress the eﬀec ts, which are due solely
113: to the time averaging, we do not use energy conservation or modiﬁe d energy functionals
114: as in the I-method. We use only the L2 norm conservation to mimic the situation which
115: occurs in the three-dimensional Euler equations and other hydrod ynamical systems.
116: Moreover, we believe that the averaging approach presented her e can be pushed further
117: to achieve the best known results concerning the KdV equation. Fu rthermore, diﬀerent
118: nonlinear dispersive and wave equations, such as the m-KdV, the Kle in-Gordon equation
119: and water wave equations (see for example, [13], [19], [23]-[25], and re ferences therein),
120: can possibly be studied quite similarly, a subject of future research .
121: 2. The Complex Burgers equation with fast rotation — a paradigm for
122: the averaging mechanism
123: In this section we consider the complex Burgers equation with fast r otation as a warmup
124: toy model to demonstrate the averaging mechanism for preventin g the formation of sin-
125: gularity.

    Title:On the regularization mechanism for the periodic Korteweg-de Vries equation

    Authors:Anatoli V. Babin, Alexei A. Ilyin, Edriss S. Titi
            View a PDF of the paper titled On the regularization mechanism for the periodic Korteweg-de Vries equation, by Anatoli V. Babin and 1 other authors

    View PDF
    HTML (experimental)



    
            Abstract:In this paper we develop and use successive averaging methods for explaining the regularization mechanism in the the periodic Korteweg--de Vries (KdV) equation in the homogeneous Sobolev spaces $\dot{H}^s$, for $s\ge0$. Specifically, we prove the global existence, uniqueness, and Lipschitz continuous dependence on the initial data of the solutions of the periodic KdV. For the case where the initial data is in $L_2$ we also show the Lipschitz continuous dependence of these solutions with respect to the initial data as maps from $\dot{H}^s$ to $\dot{H}^s$, for $s\in(-1,0]$.

                    Abstract
This article is concerned with the construction and analysis of new time discretizations for the KdV equation on a torus for low-regularity solutions below \(H^1\). New harmonic analysis tools, including averaging approximations to the exponential phase functions and trilinear estimates of the KdV operator, are established for the construction and analysis of time discretizations with higher convergence orders under low-regularity conditions. In addition, new perturbation techniques are introduced to establish stability estimates of time discretizations under low-regularity conditions without using filters when the energy techniques fail. The proposed method is proved to be convergent with order \(\gamma \) (up to a logarithmic factor) in \(L^2\) under the regularity condition \(u\in C([0,T];H^\gamma )\) for \(\gamma \in (0,1]\).

           \\n                    \\n                \\n\\n\\n                \\n\\n                    \\n                    Abstract\\nThis article is concerned with the construction and analysis of new time discretizations for the KdV equation on a torus for low-regularity solutions below \\\\(H^1\\\\). New harmonic analysis tools, including averaging approximations to the exponential phase functions and trilinear estimates of the KdV operator, are established for the construction and analysis of time discretizations with higher convergence orders under low-regularity conditions. In addition, new perturbation techniques are introduced to establish stability estimates of time discretizations under low-regularity conditions without using filters when the energy techniques fail. The proposed method is proved to be convergent with order \\\\(\\\\gamma \\\\) (up to a logarithmic factor) in \\\\(L^2\\\\) under the regularity condition \\\\(u\\\\in C([0,T];H^\\\\gamma )\\\\) for \\\\(\\\\gamma \\\\in (0,1]\\\\).\\n\\n\\n\\n\\n                    \\n\\n                    \\n    \\n\\n\\n                    \\n                        \\n                            \\n 2: 
3: This document specifies representation. Mathematical acceptance comes from
4: [Audit A's shared requirements](audit-a.md#shared-mathematical-acceptance-requirements).
5: The clean carrier binds the shared section/version/hash in execution and
6: author-readiness records; these are controller records, not extra proof axioms
7: or new fields to invent inside spec/graph.
8: 
9: New graphs/specifications use format v2 and Yui audit records use v4. The existing v1
10: Koch/BO cases are historical snapshots and have not been reaccepted. Reading
11: them requires `--legacy`; current default checks reject them. Historical
12: receipt validity is labeled `LEGACY-*` and `current_standard_receipt_valid`
13: remains false. Do not mechanically bump a version number to migrate a proof.
14: Apply [self-containment](self-containment.md) to the actual mathematical text.
15: 
16: ## Authority and semantics
17: 
18: The isolated authoring carrier offers `check_draft` and `submit_draft`, taking
19: an `artifact` JSON object directly. Prefer these to the compatible older
20: `artifact_json` string wrappers: an additional string-encoding layer is not
21: part of the mathematical format. Both routes execute identical checks.
22: 
23: `spec.json` freezes the original full theorem, the conclusion under its declared
24: parameters/hypotheses, the exact H list, global definition pairs, logic policy,
25: source-input hashes, and Lean/mathlib pins. A human must confirm that this
26: specification matches the original problem; string equality cannot establish
27: semantic fidelity. `nl0.json` references this spec by its SHA256 and duplicates
28: none of its definitions or H statements. One separate spec is required per
29: target. Multiple-target decomposition is outside version 2.
30: 
31: Read a derived proposition as a theorem under the original parameters and the
32: H nodes actually used on its derivation path. All additional free variables are
33: locally quantified in its statement; there are no ambient undeclared claims.
34: An unused original H is allowed and reported; do not silently strengthen or
35: weaken the frozen theorem. E/M results retain their general signatures; apply
36: them through explicit bindings and hypothesis checks in the inference.
37: 
38: Graph vertices are propositions and inferences. Edges are generated only as
39: `input proposition -> inference -> output proposition`. An inference requires
40: all inputs. List order is presentation only: a dependency may occur later in
41: the JSON array, provided the graph admits a topological order. Actual circular
42: dependencies, unknown IDs, and disconnected retained branches fail.
43: 
44: The isolated authoring carrier also reports a hash-bound machine checkpoint of
45: its latest own draft and actual structural result. After a context reset, resume
46: that candidate with `read_draft`/`base_candidate`; do not claim no draft exists or
47: restart the frozen input accidentally. The checkpoint grants no Audit A verdict.
48: 
49: ## Specification fields
50: 
51: Use [the authoring template](../templates/authoring.md) and the complete
52: [model-visible submission example](../templates/submission-example.md). The
53: example explains metadata placeholders and local-witness accounting; it is not
54: a benchmark or proof certification. Required top-level spec fields are:
55: 
56: - `format_version: 2`, `case_id`, `full_target`, `conclusion` (nonempty strings);
57: - `parameters`: records `{symbol, type}`; parameter symbols reserve global names.
58:   Give ambient data types/structures only. Original conditions, ranges and
59:   equations belong in H, not in parameter refinements that would be visible
60:   to every R;
61: - `hypotheses`: records `{id: Hddd, statement, origin}` extracted before authoring;
62: - `definitions`: records `{id: Dddd, symbol, definition, type, depends_on,
63:   requires, binders, objects}`. Each symbol has exactly one global meaning. `depends_on` lists
64:   earlier/resolvable D IDs and is acyclic. `requires` lists proved H/N IDs that
65:   must already be available whenever the definition is used;
66: - `logic`: `{classical: boolean, rules: [names], calculations: [fixed IDs],
67:   primitives: [{symbol, type, meaning}]}`. In the clean author tool, omit
68:   `calculations` and `primitives` to bind the controller's fixed language profile.
69:   Optional calculation IDs are `equality`, `definitions`, `finite_algebra`,
70:   `finite_order`, `finite_sums`. Optional primitive selections may be
71:   `{symbol: ...}`; the controller validates selections and binds the complete
72:   core syntax with exact type/meaning (numerals, number systems and empty-set/top
73:   notation). This is not a subject vocabulary or a list of allowed theorems. A new

325: one actual inspected location; a boolean/enum alone is insufficient.

327: Spec input hashes and source evidence are read back; malformed/duplicate JSON
328: keys, missing files, changed bytes, failed verdicts, and stale audit hashes fail.
329: 
330: Use audit `format_version: 4` for all new Yui records. A detailed-NL0 audit v3
331: cannot establish format-4 acceptance. Historical audit v1/v2 remains inspectable only
332: with historical graph v1 and --legacy, never as current acceptance.
333: Each E source review additionally has `citation_checks`, mapping exactly
334: `literature_identity`, `result_location`, `statement_fidelity`,
335: `context_completeness`, `version_and_eligibility` to separate ordinary review
336: objects `{verdict, notes, evidence}`.
337: Each version-4 inference review additionally has `external_applications`,
338: mapping exactly its E application A IDs to records
339: `{input, verdict, notes, evidence, bindings_review, hypothesis_reviews,
340: conclusion_review, bridges}`. `input` must match A's E; each nested review
341: has `{verdict, notes, evidence}`; the ordered `hypothesis_reviews` list matches
342: all source obligations one for one. `bridges` lists N nodes already in R's
343: direct input list. A bridge string is not a proof of that bridge.
344: 
345: Each inference review also has `replay: {packet_sha256, mode, carrier,
346: prior_exposure, read_materials}`. Modes are `unperformed`,
347: `same_context_diagnostic`, and `fresh_packet_only`. A passing replay/overall
348: inference requires the actual fresh carrier, empty prior proof exposure, and
349: `read_materials` equal to `["packet:<hash>"]` for mathematical input. Skill
350: instructions supply the procedure, not additional mathematics. The hash must
351: match the regenerated packet. Keep traces as evidence; metadata cannot
352: authenticate a claimed identity or prove truthful isolation.
353: 
354: Format 4 may additionally bind `review_trace:{path,sha256}` for actual tool logs.
355: This is execution metadata, not a native theorem source or an extra premise.
356: `library_evidence` contains only the successful pinned evidence of explicitly
357: retained native mathlib notes; ordinary mathematical notes require none.
358: 
359: `audit-template` creates only UNVERIFIED reviews, empty check locations and an
360: unperformed replay. It refuses to overwrite an existing output. It does not
361: inherit author notes or old verdicts. `inspect-audit` can inspect this pending
362: record; `check --audit` rejects it. Each PASS must come from actual review.
363: 
364: `check --audit` accepts only fully passing records. `inspect-audit --audit`
365: also validates the completeness and evidence of FAIL/UNVERIFIED records and
366: returns their unresolved review paths; success of inspection is not proof
367: acceptance. Overall PASS with a failed child review never passes acceptance.
368: 
369: Mode `same_context_self_audit` requires `independent: false`. If claiming an
370: independent review, disclose its actual carrier and input boundary; this file
371: does not authenticate identity or prove independence.
372: 
373: ## Local packet
374: 
375: The v2 packet contains `contract_version`, `case_id`, spec/graph hashes,
376: parameters, fixed logic, pins, expanded definitions, complete input/output
377: ports, the current inference, a warning, and `packet_sha256`. Source ports keep
378: applicability obligations and M signatures; primary-document verification is
379: separate. Producer arguments, original-proof locations, source proof text,
380: non-input H and extra ancestor/guard statements are not supplied. Guards must
381: already be direct inputs. The packet intentionally omits the global full target
382: so that its unstated premises cannot become an ambient local hypothesis.
383: 
384: Its digest is SHA256 of UTF-8 canonical JSON (`sort_keys=True`,
385: `ensure_ascii=False`, `separators=(",", ":")`) excluding `packet_sha256`.
386: It is independent of audit-verdict fields, avoiding a circular receipt hash.
387: Packets are generated views and never a second editable proof authority.
388: 
389: ## Mechanical boundaries
390: 
391: The checker validates declared objects, the frozen contract, graph closure,
392: notation-name metadata, citation parity, local-assumption accounting, guarded
393: definition availability, and hash-bound audit coverage. It verifies source
394: checkout/file hashes, not the truth of a source restatement. The printed
395: signature must be obtained from a successful pinned Lean probe and compared by
396: the auditor; an arbitrary string called `signature` is not verification.
397: 
398: The checker cannot establish that a natural-language formula is well typed,
399: that two spellings have the same mathematical meaning, that a hidden theorem
400: was not used, that a local witness did not escape the prose, or that an argument
401: is valid. Those are explicit Audit A obligations. Neither a JSON PASS nor a
402: fabricated complete audit receipt is a mathematical certificate.
403: Numbered-reference diagnostics reject common opaque references, not every
404: possible paraphrase or hidden import. Behavioral tests must actually ask an
405: auditor to review unseen controls; manually prefilled FAIL records only test
406: receipt rejection and must be reported as such.
407: 
408: ## Mathematical background receipt extension
409: 
410: New receipts declare `background_policy: "mathematical-background-v2-1"`.
411: Each R may contain background_notes with precise mathematics, local grounds and
412: actual justification; native lookup is not required. A new supplemented replay
413: uses fresh_packet_with_mathematical_background. Optional existing native notes
414: retain their complete bound library evidence; mathematical/elementary notes
415: carry no native source claim. The authored graph remains unchanged. Other
416: variant consumers must reject unsupported receipts instead of dropping fields.
417: 
418: `nl0.validate` returns the note supplement/hash and note count. A packet read
419: from an accepted source includes its notes and the original reviewed-packet
420: hash. This enriched view is not claimed to be the original replay input.
421: Translation binds the supplement in `contract.source.background_supplement_sha256`.
422: 
423: The interface source also retains the complete `background_supplement`, not
424: just its hash. Plan steps list the relevant qualified note IDs, for example
425: `background_notes:["R004.BG001"]`. Workflow freeze checks the paragraph mapping;
426: local Lean packets receive only their selected notes."}

358: 
359: `audit-template` creates only UNVERIFIED reviews, empty check locations and an
360: unperformed replay. It refuses to overwrite an existing output. It does not
361: inherit author notes or old verdicts. `inspect-audit` can inspect this pending
362: record; `check --audit` rejects it. Each PASS must come from actual review.
363: 
364: `check --audit` accepts only fully passing records. `inspect-audit --audit`
365: also validates the completeness and evidence of FAIL/UNVERIFIED records and
366: returns their unresolved review paths; success of inspection is not proof
367: acceptance. Overall PASS with a failed child review never passes acceptance.
368: 
369: Mode `same_context_self_audit` requires `independent: false`. If claiming an
370: independent review, disclose its actual carrier and input boundary; this file
371: does not authenticate identity or prove independence.
372: 
373: ## Local packet
374: 
375: The v2 packet contains `contract_version`, `case_id`, spec/graph hashes,
376: parameters, fixed logic, pins, expanded definitions, complete input/output
377: ports, the current inference, a warning, and `packet_sha256`. Source ports keep
378: applicability obligations and M signatures; primary-document verification is
379: separate. Producer arguments, original-proof locations, source proof text,
380: non-input H and extra ancestor/guard statements are not supplied. Guards must
381: already be direct inputs. The packet intentionally omits the global full target
382: so that its unstated premises cannot become an ambient local hypothesis.
383: 
384: Its digest is SHA256 of UTF-8 canonical JSON (`sort_keys=True`,
385: `ensure_ascii=False`, `separators=(",", ":")`) excluding `packet_sha256`.
386: It is independent of audit-verdict fields, avoiding a circular receipt hash.
387: Packets are generated views and never a second editable proof authority.
388: 
389: ## Mechanical boundaries
390: 
391: The checker validates declared objects, the frozen contract, graph closure,
392: notation-name metadata, citation parity, local-assumption accounting, guarded
393: definition availability, and hash-bound audit coverage. It verifies source
394: checkout/file hashes, not the truth of a source restatement. The printed
395: signature must be obtained from a successful pinned Lean probe and compared by
396: the auditor; an arbitrary string called `signature` is not verification.
397: 
398: The checker cannot establish that a natural-language formula is well typed,
399: that two spellings have the same mathematical meaning, that a hidden theorem
400: was not used, that a local witness did not escape the prose, or that an argument
401: is valid. Those are explicit Audit A obligations. Neither a JSON PASS nor a
402: fabricated complete audit receipt is a mathematical certificate.
403: Numbered-reference diagnostics reject common opaque references, not every
404: possible paraphrase or hidden import. Behavioral tests must actually ask an
405: auditor to review unseen controls; manually prefilled FAIL records only test
406: receipt rejection and must be reported as such.
407: 
408: ## Mathematical background receipt extension
409: 
410: New receipts declare `background_policy: "mathematical-background-v2-1"`.
411: Each R may contain background_notes with precise mathematics, local grounds and
412: actual justification; native lookup is not required. A new supplemented replay
413: uses fresh_packet_with_mathematical_background. Optional existing native notes
414: retain their complete bound library evidence; mathematical/elementary notes
415: carry no native source claim. The authored graph remains unchanged. Other
416: variant consumers must reject unsupported receipts instead of dropping fields.
417: 
418: `nl0.validate` returns the note supplement/hash and note count. A packet read
419: from an accepted source includes its notes and the original reviewed-packet
420: hash. This enriched view is not claimed to be the original replay input.
421: Translation binds the supplement in `contract.source.background_supplement_sha256`.
422: 
423: The interface source also retains the complete `background_supplement`, not
424: just its hash. Plan steps list the relevant qualified note IDs, for example
425: `background_notes:["R004.BG001"]`. Workflow freeze checks the paragraph mapping;
426: local Lean packets receive only their selected notes."}

target_review.notes: Compared the complete original problem, selected Theorem 1 and Section 2 standing conventions with spec and P. H001 T>0, H002 0<gamma<=1 and H003 R>0 are preserved verbatim; parameters are plain reals. P universally quantifies real mean-zero H^gamma data in the R-ball and all positive integers L after choosing C,tau0 only from T,gamma,R. It retains n=0 and n=L, tau=T/L, normalized measure, exact solution convention, full unfiltered update and uniformity in data, timestep and support. Existence/well-definedness are explicit obligations, not hidden assumptions. The declared intermediate statements preserve the covariance/two-majorant/dyadic/mixed-endpoint route and the residual, low-high, restarted bootstrap and density route in the original. This is target fidelity, not approval of R bodies.

D001.notes: The 2*pi periodic domain and normalized measure reproduce the original standing convention; no condition on T, gamma or R is encoded here.

D002.notes: The normalized Fourier coefficient and its distributional dual interpretation specify the transform used throughout; integrability is required for the integral formula.

D003.notes: All real Sobolev orders, homogeneous zero-mean norms, conjugate symmetry and zero mean are explicit. Completion defines spaces, not a solution or estimate.

D004.notes: L2, spatial Lp and sequence measures, continuous time representatives and essential-supremum derivative norms agree with the original conventions. The L2/H0 identification is the usual extension of polynomial orthogonality.

D005.notes: The Fourier multiplier fixes the sign of the Airy group for every real time and every periodic distribution; no dynamical estimate is granted.

D006.notes: The zeroth Fourier coefficient defines the mean projection for distributions and its constant-function identification.

D007.notes: The nonzero and threshold projections are explicit Fourier selectors; N>=0 is a construction domain, with no algorithmic cutoff introduced.

D008.notes: The inverse derivative has its zero mode explicitly removed, so neither inverse multiplier divides by zero; its square is specified.

D009.notes: The exact quadratic formula, including both projections, signs and coefficient 1/6, matches the original. Mean-zero L2 input and tau>0 give a legitimate formula through inverse derivatives; continuity estimates are separate N005 claims.

D010.notes: All four cubic terms match the original, including tau/9, -1/54, -1/(27*tau), bracket orientation, and S_(s-tau). Positive tau guards division. L2 inputs give f^2 in L1 and inverse-derivative factors in H1, so the products have meaning; no convergence claim is hidden.

D011.notes: The recursion and twisting use the exact fixed update on mean-zero L2, positive tau and finite L. The target's specialization tau=T/L is conditional on T>0. Well-definedness and continuity are exported by N005, not supplied as an assumption.

D012.notes: The equation, uniqueness class, smooth-approximation convention and twist are explicit. 'For such a solution' makes v and M conditional on a solution; existence and uniqueness are separately exported by N001 and asserted in P, not granted by this definition.

D013.notes: The finite average and covariance are defined for tau>0 and real phases, including zero phases. For the exponential inputs the integrals exist; no ratio estimate is included.

D014.notes: The finite polynomial Fourier sum specifies all phases, signs, excluded pair sum and zero output. Nonzero output guards 1/k. Bounded rough-input extensions are expressly deferred to N004; no boundedness is assumed.

D015.notes: The third magnitude is the third largest among all four nonzero frequencies, including the dual output. Sorting ties does not change it; its reciprocal is legitimate on the specified domain.

D016.notes: With L2 inputs the spatial product is L1 and its derivative is a distribution; conjugation by the Airy group is defined by D005. The definition supplies no product bound.

D017.notes: The bilinear inverse-derivative formula and nonzero projection are explicit. On its mean-zero L2 domain the two inverse derivatives give ordinary spatial products. Bounds and the normal-form identity remain N005 conclusions.

D018.notes: The exact nested-projection trilinear integral is initially defined for smooth inputs; rough uses are interpreted only via the stated source estimates and N006 extensions. It asserts no unsupported multiplication rule for arbitrary distributions.

D019.notes: The rational exponent 23/14 is explicit and agrees with the original continuous estimates.

D020.notes: The two components of X(I), time derivative interpretation and interval restriction are explicit. Finite X regularity is a condition in consuming propositions, not an assumed property of every function.

D021.notes: The frozen stage has the original factor 1/2, step endpoints and time-independent input; the bilinear variant is specified. Actual uses have L2, H^gamma or smooth inputs, giving the distributional integral from D016; stronger stage estimates are separately exported in N007/N009.

D022.notes: The three gamma cases, including gamma=1/2 with exponent 1/8, agree with the original. H002 is an explicit guard and is a direct input at every declared inference using this definition.

D023.notes: The complete per-step formulas reproduce the original interpolation, Q cancellation, W correction and residual concatenation. Positive tau guards division; smooth step states give the integrals (and convergent smooth Fourier remainder). Local step use is explicitly independent of a full trajectory and allows an arbitrary comparison state. Global e is conditional on an exact solution, and continuity/grid agreement are separately proved N008 assertions.

E001.notes: The combined source theorem package is faithful to the named primary results. The opposite dispersive sign is retained explicitly; the target sign/norm bridge belongs to N001/R001. No target convergence result is imported.
